SECTION I
I.	Activists and lawyers in Africa are calling for urgent action to protect women, girls and boys as
digital violence surges across the continent. A massive rise in internet users, coupled with
huge numbers of people aged under 30, has fuelled an increase in gendered online violence
across the continent, according to experts, by giving perpetrators new tools to control and
silence women and girls, and influence boys. Unfortunately, the world offline is not safe, equal
and inclusive. But the world online is proliferating that to such an extent that it’s creating a
foundation for a very, very unequal future.
In Africa, internet access is growing exponentially and more than 70% of the population of sub-
Saharan Africa is under 30. We know that young people generally face higher rates of online
violence and very often are bigger users of any tech. Digital violence against women and girls
has devastating effects such as mental health problems, withdrawal from public and economic
life, physical attacks on LGBTQI+ people in countries that criminalise homosexuality, and
femicide. While there is very little pan-African research, one study across five countries in sub-
Saharan Africa showed that 28% of women had experienced online violence. As internet access
expands, this number is expected to rise. Only 38% of people on the continent are internet
users, according to the International Telecommunication Union — and among women the figure
falls to 31%. Studies, research and anecdotal evidence at a national level paint a horrifying
picture of extreme levels of violence and a toxic online environment with dire real-life
consequences.
Extensive research conducted in Ethiopia over the past four years by the Centre for
Information Resilience (CIR) found that gendered abuse is so endemic online it has become
normalised. One Ethiopian woman interviewed by CIR said “no platform feels safe”. The
researchers found that while men are attacked online for ideas and opinions, women receive
misogynistic abuse related to their appearance and role in society. Threats and intimidation
also migrate offline, putting women at risk of physical attack.
Globally, nearly two in every five women will experience tech-facilitated violence while 85% of
women who are online have witnessed or encountered online abuse. Fewer than 40% of
countries have laws protecting women from cyber harassment or cyber stalking, leaving 44% of
the world’s women and girls — 1.8 billion — without access to legal protection. [Sociology; Word
Count: 389]

Il.	If Bazball is dead — and obituaries are being written furiously — it would be a pity. England
didn’t invent the attacking, free-flowing style, nor are they the first team to display a passion
for the game that seems to go beyond victory and defeat. The great West Indies teams of the
past played cricket with similar enthusiasm, each player expressing himself. However, Bazball
seems un-English in the land of Geoff Boycott and Alastair Cook, defensive batters of great
skill but all too aware that cricket was a livelihood and caution mattered above all.
Skipper Ben Stokes and coach Brendon ‘Baz’ McCullum see cricket as entertainment, feel they
owe something to the spectators, thoughts that would not have occurred to earlier generations.
It probably helped that they were both born in New Zealand, the land of bungee-jumping and
zorbing where it is difficult to take sports too seriously. According to Michael Brearley,
England’s high priest as successful captaincy and psychoanalyst, Bazball was born out of
depression. Stokes came through a court case (for affray), the death of his father and injury,
while McCullum, who had lost interest in the game at one time, was keen on players
rediscovering the simple joys of playing it. An awareness that asked, like Eliot, “Where is the
life we have lost in living?”
In Bazball, players “ran towards the danger”; failure didn’t mean excommunication. It has
succeeded in its three and a half years now despite the scepticism of those who believed it was
all a con. Opponents couldn’t put a finger on what Bazball was, and sometimes neither could
England. But it worked brilliantly, with England winning Tests with fabulous fourth-innings
chases against Pakistan, New Zealand and India. The sight of Joe Root reverse scooping fast

bowlers for six seemed to give Bazball the final stamp of approval from one of the greats who
swore by established technique.
Perhaps Bazball is best enjoyed by those who have no skin in the game. It is glorious cricket
for those outside England who are not so invested in the result. Would an Indian batter be
forgiven for getting out repeatedly because he kept making the same mistake, although on
other occasions the identical shot fetched tons of runs and encomiums?
To enjoy, even encourage an approach when it works but call it ‘stupid’ when it fails is bad
faith.
[Sports; Word Count: 392]

IV.	According to media theorist Marshall McLuhan, every medium is an extension of our physical
or mental faculties. The hammer extends our fist, the spear our teeth, the hut our skin, the
wheel our feet — and electronic media extend our central nervous system to all of humankind.
Extended abilities give us new powers but disrupt previous sensory, cognitive, and social
settings. As humankind switched to the internet, printing no longer defines the protocols
humans live by. Print-based culture is collapsing. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The era of printing was, in fact, very short by historical standards — about 550 years. Some
call this period the Gutenberg Parenthesis — a metaphor popularized by Jeff Jarvis. Within
this Parenthesis, communication was centered around fixed, authored, linear, and stable texts.
Things were different before books. Communication was fluid and situational, passed mostly
through direct interaction between people. The internet has largely restored those conditions:
digital content is updated, shared, and much of it is user-generated — just like in orality.
Books withdrew both author and reader from the surrounding reality and turned them inward,
into contemplation. Before literacy, it was different — people were immersed in the flow of
events. This pattern returns: people are once again immersed in a flow — this time, a digital
one.

situational immersion typical of orality, not only is the Gutenberg Parenthesis closing, but the
metaphor of a closing parenthesis — or arc — can be extended to the entire era of literacy. The
environmental detachment as a media effect appeared before print — it was the effect of
writing. Writing separated the known from the knower (Havelock) and made it possible to
contemplate things “from outside” interaction with them.

thinker. Writing made this possible by putting words before the individual for contemplation.

XII. The 42nd Amendment of the Constitution of India, enacted in 1976 during the Emergency, is
one of the most far-reaching constitutional amendments in Indian history and is often
described as the “Mini-Constitution.” Its background lies in the political turbulence of the
1970s, particularly after the Golaknath case (1967), which intensified conflict between the
judiciary and the executive over Parliament’s amending power. The Allahabad High Court
judgment against Prime Minister Indira Gandhi for election malpractice further deepened the
crisis. After the declaration of Emergency on 25 June 1975, the government acquired
extraordinary powers and introduced several constitutional changes, of which the 42nd
Amendment was the most comprehensive. Its objectives were to strengthen executive power,
curtail judicial review, enhance Parliament’s authority, centralise administration, and reshape
the Constitution in line with the government’s political and ideological agenda.
The amendment introduced sweeping changes across the Constitution. In the Preamble, it
added the words “Socialist” and “Secular” and changed “unity of the nation” to “unity and

integrity of the nation.” It expanded the Directive Principles of State Policy by inserting
Articles 39A, 43A, and 48A, dealing with free legal aid, workers’ participation in management,
and environmental protection, and amended Article 39(f) for child welfare. It also inserted Part
IV-A, introducing Fundamental Duties of citizens. In the Seventh Schedule, subjects such as
education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and
administration of justice were shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List, increasing
central control. It formalised the rule that the President must act on the advice of the Cabinet,
inserted Article 257A to allow deployment of central forces in states, abolished quorum
requirements in legislatures, and extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
from five years to six years. The amendment also altered emergency provisions, allowed
national emergency to apply to the whole or part of India, extended the duration of President’s
Rule, restricted High Courts’ jurisdiction, required a seven-judge bench with a two-thirds
majority in certain constitutional cases, inserted Part XIV-A with Articles 323A and 323B for
tribunals, and expanded the operation of Article 358 for suspension of Article 19 rights during
emergencies.
The amendment faced strong criticism for weakening democracy, federalism, and judicial
independence. In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down
important parts of the amendment, especially provisions that gave Parliament unlimited
amending power and curtailed judicial review, and reaffirmed the Basic Structure Doctrine.
After the Emergency, the 43rd and 44th Amendments reversed many of its excesses. Thus, the
42nd Amendment remains a landmark example of both constitutional overreach and the
resilience of judicial review in India.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, https://lawbhoomi.com/42nd-amendment-of-
indian-constitution/

newer pocket Constitution, printed after the Emergency-era “Mini-Constitution,” containing

options.text:
It removed “Sovereign” and “Democratic” and inserted “Federal” and “Presidential”,

It inserted a new clause making elections optional during Emergency and changed “We,

options.text:
It added the words “Socialist” and “Secular” and changed “unity of the nation” to “unity

no political purpose. Another student counters that its design during the Emergency sought to
recalibrate power among institutions and reduce judicial checking. The professor asks the class

Which objective-set most closely captures the intended direction of change?

circular stating that Article 19 freedoms stand suspended in those districts, and a detained
journalist’s writ petition in the High Court is dismissed as “not maintainable” on the ground

National emergency could apply to the whole or part of India, and Article 358 was
expanded to suspend Article 19 rights during emergencies.

Emergency could apply only to the whole of India, and Article 19 rights could never be
suspended even during emergencies anywhere.

options.text:
High Courts retained full jurisdiction always, and constitutional benches required only
three judges with a simple majority in every case.

options.label: d
options.text:
President’s Rule was reduced in duration, and tribunals were abolished, so all
constitutional disputes had to go to civil courts only.

machinery to ensure uninterrupted rule, including changes affecting the President,
legislatures, and security deployment in states. Years later, a civics student reads this article

Which change should the student attribute to that amendment?

It reduced Lok Sabha term to four years, restored quorum rules, and barred central forces

It mandated the President act independently of the Cabinet, removed Article 257A, and

It extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies from five years to six years

A law student argues that the 1976 amendment (424 Amendment) permanently made
Parliament supreme by removing meaningful judicial review over constitutional changes. Her
senior replies that a later famous Supreme Court decision struck down key parts that tried to
give Parliament unlimited amending power and to curtail judicial review, reaffirming a
structural limitation doctrine. The student is asked to name the decision and the holding that
answers this debate.
Which option most directly matches that judicial response?

options.text:
Golaknath (1967) struck down the amendment entirely, restored judicial review, and
declared Parliament has no power to amend any provision at all.

options.label: b
options.text:
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) approved unlimited amending power, removed basic structure
limits, and barred courts from reviewing constitutional amendments thereafter
permanently in India.

options.label: c
options.text:
Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) upheld the amendment, validated curbs on judicial review,
and extended legislative terms, holding elections need not be fair.

options.label: d

Minerva Mills (1980) struck down important parts giving Parliament unlimited amending
power and curtailing judicial review, reaffirming the Basic Structure Doctrine again.

XII. Mens rea means the guilty mental state that ordinarily accompanies a criminal act. This
article explains it through the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: an act does not
make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty. It notes that mens rea was not always
treated as an ingredient of crime; in earlier periods, punishment could follow even without
proof of intention. Over time, especially from the seventeenth century onward, criminal law
came to recognise that blameworthy conduct usually requires both a wrongful act and a
blameworthy state of mind. In India, this idea entered criminal law through English influence
and became reflected across the Indian Penal Code, even though the phrase “mens rea” itself is
not expressly used in the Code. The article points out that many IPC offences use words such
as “voluntarily,” “dishonestly,” “knowingly,” and “fraudulently,” which embody the idea of a
guilty mind.
The passage identifies four main forms of mens rea: intention, knowledge, recklessness, and
negligence. Intention refers to a deliberate mental decision to bring about a consequence;
knowledge refers to awareness of facts and likely consequences; recklessness means foreseeing
a risk but proceeding with indifference to it; and negligence is failure to exercise the degree of
care that a prudent person would have used in the circumstances. It also emphasises that
mens rea is usually essential in criminal law unless a statute expressly or by necessary
implication excludes it. The Supreme Court decisions discussed, such as Ravule Hariprasada
Rao v. State and State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George, support the principle that guilty
mind is generally presumed to be a component of criminal liability unless legislation clearly
rules it out.
Another key point in the article is the need for concurrence of mens rea and actus reus: the
guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together for criminal liability in the ordinary case.

Mere intention without the act, or the act without the corresponding guilty state of mind, will
not usually be enough. At the same time, it notes important exceptions, especially strict
liability offences, where proof of mens rea is not required. Examples listed include criminal
libel, public nuisance, contempt of court, kidnapping/abduction, bigamy, rape, sale of obscene
books, and certain statutory offences under laws such as the Essential Commodities Act and
the Motor Vehicles Act. The overall conclusion of the article is that mens rea remains a
foundational idea in criminal law, but its role depends on the language, structure, and purpose
of the particular offence.

know-about-mens-rea/

Kunal angrily writes in his diary that he intends to burn his neighbour’s shed “next weekend.”
Two days later, while Kunal is out of town, a short circuit in the neighbour’s shed causes a fire
and the shed burns down. Police find Kunal’s diary during a separate inquiry and arrest him
for the burning, claiming his written intention proves guilt. Kunal argues he never performed
any act leading to the fire and was not even present.
How should liability be assessed on these facts?

Kunal is liable because intention alone proves guilt, and the diary entry substitutes for the
act when harm eventually occurs later.

options.text:
Kunal is liable because presence is irrelevant, and any earlier intention attaches to later
events, even if caused independently by accident.

options.text:
Kunal is not liable because the guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together, and
here the act occurred without his mind.

options.label: d
options.text:
Kunal is not liable because diaries are privileged, so courts cannot ever use them, even if
they show intent to commit crime.

A delivery driver, Neel, sees a bright warning sign that a bridge ahead is under repair and
may collapse under heavy vehicles. He thinks, “It will probably be fine,” and drives his loaded
truck across anyway to save time. The bridge collapses, causing injury. Neel claims he did not
desire the collapse and therefore lacked intention. The prosecution argues that he foresaw a
risk and proceeded with indifference to it.
Which mental state most closely fits his conduct as described?

options.label: a
options.text:
Intention, because he deliberately drove, so he must be treated as wanting the collapse
outcome, regardless of what he believed.

options.label: b
options.text:
Knowledge, because he was fully certain collapse would occur, and acted with awareness
that the consequence would happen inevitably anyway.

options.label: c
options.text:
Recklessness, because he foresaw a risk but proceeded with indifference to it, treating the
warning as ignorable for convenience.

options.label: d
options.text:
Negligence, because he had no awareness at all, and only failed to take care due to
momentary forgetfulness, not risk-taking.

questions.stem:
A newspaper editor publishes a harsh, false article accusing a citizen of corruption, believing the
allegation to be true because a source told him so. The citizen sues and also seeks criminal action,
and the editor argues he lacked any guilty mind because he honestly believed the claim and had no
intention to harm. The complainant replies that certain offences do not require proof of mens rea
and are treated as strict liability in law.
Which statement best reflects the passage’s point about exceptions?

options.text:
The editor must be acquitted because mens rea is always essential, and honest belief
automatically defeats every criminal offence in all cases.

options.label: b
options.text:
The editor may still face liability because strict liability offences exist where proof of mens rea
is not required, as it is an exception.

options.label: c
options.text:
The editor must be acquitted because strict liability applies only to traffic violations, and never
to publication-related offences in criminal law.

options.label: d
options.text:
The editor must be acquitted because civil suits are the only remedy for publications, and
criminal law never recognises any publication offence.

believing it is her own. Thirty minutes later, she opens it in a taxi, realises it belongs to someone

How should liability be approached?

Liable because negligence is enough for dishonest taking, and confusion about bags still shows

Not liable because mens rea means a guilty mental state accompanying a criminal act, and her

A statute regulating export documents states: “Whoever brings prohibited goods into India in
breach of notification shall be punished,” without mentioning “knowingly” or “intentionally.” Riya, a
passenger, is caught with a sealed package placed in her bag by a travel agent, and she claims she
did not know it contained prohibited goods. The prosecution argues that because the statute is
silent on intention, guilt is automatic and knowledge is irrelevant. Riya argues guilty mind is
normally presumed unless the law clearly rules it out.
Which position best matches the passage principle?

options.label: a
options.text:
Defence barred: statutory silence always excludes mens rea; liability becomes automatic for
every offence, so knowledge is irrelevant.

options.label: b
options.text:
Defence considered: guilty mind is generally presumed unless legislation clearly rules it out,
though words like knowingly are absent here.

XII. Mens rea means the guilty mental state that ordinarily accompanies a criminal act. This
article explains it through the maxim actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: an act does not
make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty. It notes that mens rea was not always
treated as an ingredient of crime; in earlier periods, punishment could follow even without
proof of intention. Over time, especially from the seventeenth century onward, criminal law
came to recognise that blameworthy conduct usually requires both a wrongful act and a
blameworthy state of mind. In India, this idea entered criminal law through English influence
and became reflected across the Indian Penal Code, even though the phrase “mens rea” itself is
not expressly used in the Code. The article points out that many IPC offences use words such
as “voluntarily,” “dishonestly,” “knowingly,” and “fraudulently,” which embody the idea of a
guilty mind.
The passage identifies four main forms of mens rea: intention, knowledge, recklessness, and
negligence. Intention refers to a deliberate mental decision to bring about a consequence;
knowledge refers to awareness of facts and likely consequences; recklessness means foreseeing
a risk but proceeding with indifference to it; and negligence is failure to exercise the degree of
care that a prudent person would have used in the circumstances. It also emphasises that
mens rea is usually essential in criminal law unless a statute expressly or by necessary
implication excludes it. The Supreme Court decisions discussed, such as Ravule Hariprasada
Rao v. State and State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George, support the principle that guilty
mind is generally presumed to be a component of criminal liability unless legislation clearly
rules it out.
Another key point in the article is the need for concurrence of mens rea and actus reus: the
guilty mind and the wrongful act must exist together for criminal liability in the ordinary case.

Mere intention without the act, or the act without the corresponding guilty state of mind, will
not usually be enough. At the same time, it notes important exceptions, especially strict
liability offences, where proof of mens rea is not required. Examples listed include criminal
libel, public nuisance, contempt of court, kidnapping/abduction, bigamy, rape, sale of obscene
books, and certain statutory offences under laws such as the Essential Commodities Act and
the Motor Vehicles Act. The overall conclusion of the article is that mens rea remains a
foundational idea in criminal law, but its role depends on the language, structure, and purpose
of the particular offence.

know-about-mens-rea/

XIV. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to
guardian and ward. Before this legislation, guardianship matters were governed by different
personal laws and judicial practices. The Act introduced a uniform procedural framework with
the objective of providing a judicial mechanism for appointment and declaration of guardians,
protecting the person and property of minors, regulating the powers, duties, and liabilities of
guardians, preventing misuse of a minor’s property, and ensuring that the welfare of the minor
remains the controlling consideration. The Act extends to the whole of India and applies to all
minors under the Indian Majority Act, 1875, that is, ordinarily persons below 18 years, and
covers guardians of the person, property, or both. It becomes relevant in situations such as
death of parents, custody disputes, divorce or separation, management of minor’s property,
appointment of a guardian, or removal of an existing guardian. Though it does not override
specific adoption laws, guardianship disputes may still come within its scope.
Section 4 defines the key expressions: a minor is a person who has not attained majority, a
guardian is a person having care of the person or property of a minor or both, a ward is a
minor for whom there is a guardian, and the Court generally means the District Court having
jurisdiction. The Act is divided into four chapters dealing with preliminary matters,
appointment and declaration of guardians, duties and liabilities of guardians, and
supplemental provisions. Under Section 7, the Court may appoint or declare a guardian where
necessary for the welfare of the minor. Under Section 8, applications may be made by a
proposed guardian, a relative or friend, the Collector, or any authorised person. Section 9
governs jurisdiction, Section 10 prescribes the contents of the application, and Section 12
empowers the Court to issue interim orders for production, custody, or protection of property.
The most important provision is Section 17, which makes the welfare of the minor the guiding
principle and requires the Court to consider factors such as age, sex, religion, character and
capacity of the proposed guardian, nearness of kin, wishes of a deceased parent, and even the

intelligent preference of the minor if old enough. Section 19 places restrictions on appointment
where fit natural guardians are living.
Chapter III regulates the duties, rights, and liabilities of guardians. Under Section 20, the
guardian stands in a fiduciary position toward the ward. Sections 24 to 26 deal with the
guardian of the person, who is responsible for custody, support, health, education, and cannot
remove the minor from jurisdiction without permission. Sections 27, 29, and 31 deal with
guardians of property, requiring ordinary prudence in management and court permission
before sale, mortgage, transfer, or long lease of immovable property.

A 14-year-old ward, Arman, owns a small apartment inherited from his mother. His current
guardian, a distant cousin, begins negotiating a quick sale and tells neighbours he will “finalise it
this week.” Arman’s school principal learns this and informs the court that Arman is being
pressured to sign papers. A relative files an urgent request asking the court to immediately stop
any sale and to secure the property documents until a full guardianship inquiry is completed. The
guardian argues nothing can be done until final appointment proceedings end.
What can the court do at this stage?

options.text:
Court may issue interim orders for custody or protection of property so documents and
possession can be secured immediately to prevent misuse.

The court cannot pass any interim order because guardianship disputes require a full trial first,

options.text:
Court may only punish the guardian criminally, because civil courts cannot interfere with
property negotiations unless fraud is already proved fully.

options.label: d
options.text:
The court must allow the sale because guardians have absolute property powers, and minors’
property can be disposed of without court supervision.

questions.stem:
Rina is appointed guardian of her nephew Dev (a minor) and is given control over Dev’s rental
income. Rina starts depositing the rent into her personal account and uses it to fund her own
business expansion, promising that she will “repay later with profit.” Dev’s grandmother challenges
this conduct and seeks the court’s intervention, arguing that a guardian must not treat the ward’s
money as personal capital. Rina argues she is “family” and acted in Dev’s best interest by investing.
What is the best legal view?

options.label: a
options.text:
Guardian stands in a fiduciary position toward the ward, so personal use of the ward’s funds
breaches the duty even if repayment is promised.

options.label: b
options.text:
Guardian is like an owner of the ward’s income, so using it for personal business is allowed as
long as some benefit is intended.

options.label: c
options.text:
Guardian owes only moral duties, not legal ones, so court cannot intervene unless the guardian
admits dishonesty in writing first.

options.label: d
options.text:
A guardian may freely invest the ward’s money in any venture without constraints, because
family relationships remove fiduciary duties altogether.

After a divorce, both parents are alive but dispute custody and education decisions for their 9-
year-old child. The father claims the mother is unfit and seeks a court declaration appointing
him as guardian of the person, while the mother says she already has custody and no
“appointment” is needed because both are natural parents. The court is asked to intervene
formally to settle authority and reduce conflict.
Under what condition can the court appoint or declare a guardian in such a situation?

options.text:
The court may appoint a guardian only when relatives consent unanimously, because
courts cannot interfere in parental disputes without family agreement.

options.label: b
options.text:
The court may appoint a guardian only if both parents die, because living parents always
bar the court from making any declaration.

The court may appoint a guardian only if the minor owns property, because guardianship

Court may appoint or declare a guardian where necessary for the welfare of the minor,
even if parents dispute custody and control.

A guardian of property, Suresh, wants to sell the minor ward’s agricultural land because he
believes land prices will fall soon. He executes a sale deed to a third party without approaching
the court, saying it is “urgent business judgment.” The purchaser argues he paid fair market

How should this dispute be approached?

Court permission required before sale or transfer of minor’s immovable property, so sale

options.text:

XV. Malicious prosecution under the law of tort means the wrongful institution of legal
proceedings, usually criminal, against a person without reasonable and probable cause and
with a malicious intention. The iPleaders article explains that Black’s Law Dictionary defines
it as a legal proceeding initiated without probable cause and with harmful intent, and the
Supreme Court in West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray (2006) described it
as misuse of the legal system to harm another person without valid justification. The article
also distinguishes malicious prosecution from abuse of process and abuse of power. Malicious
prosecution concerns the wrongful starting of proceedings at the very beginning, whereas
abuse of process refers to misuse of a legal process after it has been properly initiated, and
abuse of power concerns misuse of official authority outside the courtroom context.

The article identifies five essential elements that a plaintiff must prove in an action for
malicious prosecution: prosecution by the defendant, absence of reasonable and probable cause,
malice, termination of proceedings in favour of the plaintiff, and damage suffered by the
plaintiff. “Prosecution” is used in a wider sense than a trial and can include criminal
proceedings by way of appeal or revision, though the article notes that mere proceedings before
a police officer have been held not to amount to prosecution, while the position regarding

Complainant relied on clear CCTV and a written confession; that supplies a justified basis, even if

immediately, the contractor files a criminal complaint alleging Rohit stole tools, even though

Malice requires personal spite alone, so unless the builder hated the owner personally, the

Malice exists whenever the police investigate, because starting any complaint shows
hostility, and courts presume malicious intention from litigation.

colleague. She was arrested at school, suspended for three months, and local newspapers
reported the allegation. The criminal court later discharged her without any finding of guilt.
Farida files a tort suit and must show actual damage rather than relying on hurt feelings
alone. She claims her reputation suffered, her liberty was restrained, and she spent money on
legal defence.
Which description best captures the kinds of damage recognised for this tort?

options.label: a
options.text:
Damage may be to reputation, person, or property, so arrest humiliation, medical stress,
and legal fees can satisfy actual damage.

options.label: b
options.text:
Damage is presumed from acquittal alone, so the plaintiff need not show any injury to
reputation, person, or property.

options.label: c
options.text:
Only physical injury counts as damage, so reputational harm and litigation costs are
irrelevant to malicious prosecution actions in tort.

options.label: d
options.text:
Only property loss counts as damage, so arrest and stigma cannot be considered even if
proceedings ended favourably for plaintiff.

SECTION IV
XVI. In the late 20th century, the world came together to plug a hole in the ozone layer — the part
of Earth’s atmosphere that absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation. If left
unchecked, this hole would have exposed life on Earth to dangerous — and in some regions
potentially lethal — levels of radiation, but an international treaty brought us back from the
brink of disaster. That treaty, the Montreal Protocol, is a lesson in human resilience: We can
save the world, because we already did it once before.
The story of the Montreal Protocol starts, bizarrely, with an epidemic of deadly fridges in the
1920s. In those pioneer days of electric home refrigeration, everyone’s favorite new kitchen
appliance relied on highly toxic, flammable, or corrosive gases to keep food chilled. A faulty
compressor or leaky pipe could wipe out an entire family in their sleep, and in the first half of
1929, gas from fridges killed at least 15 people in Chicago alone.
Danger drove innovation, and in 1928, General Motors engineer Thomas Midgley Jr.
synthesized the first chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) — a cheap, non-toxic, non-flammable gas
marketed in the U.S. under the brand name Freon. CFCs seemed miraculous, and post-war
consumers fell in love with them. They became the coolant in every refrigerator and air
conditioner in the world, as well as the propellant of choice in billions of aerosol cans, ejecting
hairspray, deodorant, whipped cream, and countless other consumables, all at the push of a
button. But CFCs, the solution to an earlier problem, turned out to be villains in disguise. In
1974, University of California scientists F. Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina asked an
inconvenient question: Where do all the CFCs go?
Because CFC molecules are so stable, they don’t break down in the lower atmosphere.
Rowland and Molina hypothesized that they drifted upward into the stratosphere, 10 to 30
miles above the Earth’s surface, where they would be smashed apart by the Sun’s ultraviolet
(UV) rays. This releases chlorine atoms — like a microscopic, demented Pac-Man, a single one
can devour more than 100,000 ozone molecules.
If their hypothesis were correct, that would be catastrophic. The ozone layer is like Earth’s
sunscreen: It lets through most of the Sun’s relatively benign UV-A rays, absorbs most of the
harmful UV-B, and blocks all of the even more dangerous UV-C radiation. Without the ozone
layer, those unwelcome UV rays would reach Earth’s surface, where they'd mutate DNA,
cause skin cancers and cataracts, and kill crops and marine ecosystems. Fellow scientists were
skeptical of the theory, while the chemical industry was downright hostile. [Sci-Tech; Word
Count: 431]
